Wilson Goode :: Early life :: chunk_0001
Goode was born into a family of [tenant farmers](/wiki/Tenant_farmer "Tenant farmer") near [Seaboard, North Carolina](/wiki/Seaboard,_North_Carolina "Seaboard, North Carolina").[[1]](#cite_note-1) His family arrived in Philadelphia in 1953 and lived in the [Paschall](/wiki/Paschall,_Philadelphia "Paschall, Philadelphia") neighborhood in [Southwest Philadelphia](/wiki/Southwest_Philadelphia "Southwest Philadelphia"). He was an honors student at [John Bartram High School](/wiki/John_Bartram_High_School "John Bartram High School") and then he graduated from [Morgan State University](/wiki/Morgan_State_University "Morgan State University") in 1961. He was a member of the Reserve Officers Training Corps while attending Morgan State and entered the [US Army](/wiki/United_States_Army "United States Army") as a First Lieutenant in the military police. He returned to Philadelphia and briefly worked as a manager at a building maintenance firm and as an insurance adjuster before he was hired by the Philadelphia Council for Community Development in 1967. He became executive director of PCCD in 1971. In 1967 he and his wife bought a house in the Paschall neighborhood, where he served as a deacon of Paschall's First Baptist Church. In 1968, he completed his graduate studies at the [Fels Institute of Government](/wiki/Fels_Institute_of_Government "Fels Institute of Government") at the [University of Pennsylvania](/wiki/University_of_Pennsylvania "University of Pennsylvania") where he earned his master's in Public Administration.[[2]](#cite_note-2)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/ca/Wesolin.jpg/250px-Wesolin.jpg)](/wiki/File:Wesolin.jpg)

The view from Foss Hill: From left to right: Judd Hall, Harriman Hall (which houses the Public Affairs Center), and [Olin Memorial Library](/wiki/Olin_Memorial_Library "Olin Memorial Library")

Wesleyan occupies a 360-acre (1.5 km2) campus, with over 340 buildings, including the five-building College Row; Olin Memorial Library; Andrus Public Affairs Center; the Exley Science Center; Shanklin and Hall-Atwater Laboratories; the [Van Vleck Observatory](/wiki/Van_Vleck_Observatory "Van Vleck Observatory"); Fayerweather with Beckham Hall; Russell House, a National Historic Landmark; the Allbritton Center; the Butterfield dormitories; the Fauver Field dormitories; and the 11-building Center for the Arts complex.

When Wesleyan University was founded in 1831, it took over a campus with two buildings, North College and South College, from 1825. These were originally constructed by the City of Middletown for use by Captain Partridge's American Literary, Scientific, and Military Academy. In 1829, after the Connecticut legislature declined it a charter to grant college degrees, Partridge moved his academy to [Northfield, Vermont](/wiki/Northfield,_Vermont "Northfield, Vermont"). The academy later became [Norwich University](/wiki/Norwich_University "Norwich University") and the Middletown buildings were acquired by Wesleyan.

The original North College was destroyed in a fire in 1906, but South College survived, being converted into offices that same year. The cupola and the belfry, which contains the Wesleyan Carillon, was designed by [Henry Bacon](/wiki/Henry_Bacon "Henry Bacon") and was added in 1916.[[30]](#cite_note-30)

fanoutqa_016180.x:
Bill Gates :: Microsoft :: IBM partnership :: chunk_0006
[IBM](/wiki/IBM "IBM"), the leading supplier of computer equipment to commercial enterprises at the time, approached Microsoft in July 1980 concerning software for its upcoming personal computer, the [IBM PC](/wiki/IBM_PC "IBM PC"),[[39]](#cite_note-bunnell1982febmar-40) after Gates's mother mentioned Microsoft to [John Opel](/wiki/John_Opel "John Opel"), IBM's then [CEO](/wiki/CEO "CEO").[[4]](#cite_note-mary-maxwell-gates-obit-5) IBM first proposed that Microsoft write the BASIC interpreter. IBM's representatives also mentioned that they needed an operating system, and Gates referred them to [Digital Research](/wiki/Digital_Research "Digital Research") (DRI), makers of the widely used [CP/M](/wiki/CP/M "CP/M") operating system.[[40]](#cite_note-41) IBM's discussions with Digital Research went poorly, and they did not reach a licensing agreement. IBM representative Jack Sams mentioned the licensing difficulties during a subsequent meeting with Gates and asked if Microsoft could provide an operating system. A few weeks later, Gates and Allen proposed using [86-DOS](/wiki/86-DOS "86-DOS"), an operating system similar to CP/M, that [Tim Paterson](/wiki/Tim_Paterson "Tim Paterson") of [Seattle Computer Products](/wiki/Seattle_Computer_Products "Seattle Computer Products") (SCP) had made for hardware similar to the PC.[[41]](#cite_note-42) Microsoft made a deal with SCP to be the exclusive licensing agent of 86-DOS, and later the full owner. Microsoft employed Paterson to adapt the operating system for the PC[[42]](#cite_note-43) and delivered it to IBM as [PC DOS](/wiki/PC_DOS "PC DOS") for a one-time fee of $50,000.[[43]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGates199654-44)

The contract itself only earned Microsoft a relatively small fee. It was the prestige brought to Microsoft by IBM's adoption of its operating system that would be the origin of Microsoft's transformation from a small business to the leading software company i

fanoutqa_035124.x:
Brooklyn Technical High School :: History :: Recent years :: Randy Asher :: chunk_0008
On February 7, 2006, the Department of Education named Randy Asher, founding principal of the [High School for Math, Science and Engineering](/wiki/High_School_for_Math,_Science_and_Engineering "High School for Math, Science and Engineering") (HSMSE), as interim acting principal.[[31]](#cite_note-32) Asher had previously served as Brooklyn Tech's assistant principal in mathematics from 2000 to 2002 before leaving to become founding principal of HSMSE. During his time as principal, the total student enrollment increased from 4,200 to 5,700.[[32]](#cite_note-NY_Daily_News-33) In the beginning of January 2017, Asher abruptly left Tech to take on a new position as an NYC Education Department senior advisor to help reduce the [Absent Teacher Reserve](/wiki/Absent_Teacher_Reserve "Absent Teacher Reserve").[[32]](#cite_note-NY_Daily_News-33) Throughout Asher's tenure, the school's reputation was sullied by several allegations of sexual harassment and assault of students by faculty members, resulting in the termination of Sean Shaynak (an aerospace engineering teacher hired by Asher) and the reassignment of English teacher and school newspaper advisor David Lo.[[33]](#cite_note-34)[[34]](#cite_note-35) The school was also rocked by allegations of racism against black students and Asher faced mounting student pressure on social media to fix the situation.[[35]](#cite_note-36) Following Asher's departure, former assistant principal David Newman took on the new position as acting principal of the specialized high school. In February 2020, Newman was appointed principal.[[36]](#cite_note-37)

Lee High School (Midland, Texas)") in Midland and finished his high-school playing career with 8,423 rushing yards (the most in Texas 5A history, largest classification at the time and the fourth-most in Texas [high school football](/wiki/High_school_football "High school football") history).[[1]](#cite_note-1) He led his team to three consecutive state championships and rushed for a total of 15 touchdowns in the three championship games. Benson rushed for more than 1,900 yards in only nine games. He rushed for over 3,500 yards (51 touchdowns) during his junior year, when his team went undefeated and won state and national championships. He became the first high-school player to appear on the cover of the *[Dave Campbell's Texas Football](/wiki/Dave_Campbell%27s_Texas_Football "Dave Campbell's Texas Football")* annual magazine. Benson was also a [center fielder](/wiki/Center_fielder "Center fielder") on the [baseball](/wiki/Baseball "Baseball") team. The court lacked its own building until 1935. For most of that time, it had chambers in the [Capitol Building](/wiki/United_States_Capitol "United States Capitol") in [Washington, D.C.](/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C.") Prior to that, between 1791 and 1801, the court met in [City Hall](/wiki/Old_City_Hall_(Philadelphia) "Old City Hall (Philadelphia)") (pictured) in [Philadelphia](/wiki/Philadelphia "Philadelphia").

In 1787, four years after the end of the [American Revolutionary War](/wiki/American_Revolutionary_War "American Revolutionary War"), delegates to the [1787 Constitutional Convention](/wiki/Constitutional_Convention_(United_States) "Constitutional Convention (United States)") convened in [Philadelphia](/wiki/Philadelphia "Philadelphia"), where they debated the [separation of powers](/wiki/Separation_of_powers "Separation of powers") between the legislative and executive departments and established parameters for a [national judiciary](/wiki/Judicial_branch "Judicial branch")[[8]](#cite_note-8) as a third branch of the [federal government](/wiki/Federal_government_of_the_United_States "Federal government of the United States"). View above Camp-IV of K2

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/0/07/K2_West_1909.jpg/250px-K2_West_1909.jpg)](/wiki/File:K2_West_1909.jpg)

The west face of K2 taken from the Savoia Glacier, on the 1909 expedition

The mountain was first surveyed by a British team in 1856. Team member [Thomas Montgomerie](/wiki/Thomas_George_Montgomerie "Thomas George Montgomerie") designated the mountain "K2" for being the second peak of the Karakoram range. The other peaks were originally named K1, K3, K4, and K5, but were eventually renamed [Masherbrum](/wiki/Masherbrum "Masherbrum"), [Gasherbrum IV](/wiki/Gasherbrum_IV "Gasherbrum IV"), [Gasherbrum II](/wiki/Gasherbrum_II "Gasherbrum II"), and [Gasherbrum I](/wiki/Gasherbrum_I "Gasherbrum I"), respectively.[[39]](#cite_note-42) In 1892, [Martin Conway](/wiki/Martin_Conway,_1st_Baron_Conway_of_Allington "Martin Conway, 1st Baron Conway of Allington") led a British expedition that reached "[Concordia](/wiki/Concordia_(Karakoram) "Concordia (Karakoram)")" on the [Baltoro Glacier](/wiki/Baltoro_Glacier "Baltoro Glacier").[[40]](#cite_note-43)

The first serious attempt to climb K2 was undertaken in 1902 by [Oscar Eckenstein](/wiki/Oscar_Eckenstein "Oscar Eckenstein"), [Aleister Crowley](/wiki/Aleister_Crowley "Aleister Crowley"), [Jules Jacot-Guillarmod](/wiki/Jules_Jacot-Guillarmod "Jules Jacot-Guillarmod"), Heinrich Pfannl, Victor Wessely, and [Guy Knowles](/wiki/Guy_Knowles "Guy Knowles") via the Northeast Ridge. As of 2017 Singapore's GDP reached $323.907 billion.[[74]](#cite_note-76)

Singapore is expected to experience an economic slowdown in 2019, with GDP growth slowing to 1.9% from 3.1% in 2018, due to tariff hikes from the United States and China.[[75]](#cite_note-77)

During the initial months of the [COVID-19 pandemic](/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic"), on 26 March 2020, Singapore's Ministry of Trade and Industry said it believed that the economy would contract by between 1% and 4% in 2020. This was after the economy shrank 2.2% in the first quarter of 2020 from the same quarter in 2019.[[76]](#cite_note-78) On 26 May, MTI said that it was revising down its expectation for the Singapore economy in 2020 to shrink by 4% to 7%.[[77]](#cite_note-79) Economists had to downgrade their numbers from previously, and some suggested that the economic recovery could take some time.[[78]](#cite_note-80)[[79]](#cite_note-81) In response to the economic pressure, Moody's temporarily downgraded the Singapore banking sector that year from "stable" outlook to a "negative" outlook.[[80]](#cite_note-82)
